hook: Did you know ancient Egypt's highest military award for battlefield bravery was a set of golden flies?
article: In 1859, excavators unburied the sealed wooden coffin of Queen Ahhotep containing three glittering golden flies. While ordinary housefly amulets were popular symbolic items, actual golden flies served as the military's highest award for battlefield bravery.

Remarkably, none of the fourteen fine inscribed artifacts found inside the coffin actually bore Queen Ahhotep's own name. Five objects explicitly bore the name of King Kamose, while seven items were attributed to the young pharaoh Ahmose I.

These golden flies stood as an eternal symbol of persistent, unyielding military service on the battlefield. Though her physical mummy was destroyed after discovery, these precious artifacts endure as an ultimate badge of ancient combat bravery.
engage: What detail surprised you most about a royal queen being buried with battlefield bravery awards?
author: Rob Corder

hook: Imagine stepping into a dark ancient tomb and having sixty golden faces suddenly stare back at you.
article: As excavations began in 1999, archaeologists uncovered a massive necropolis estimated to hold over ten thousand mummies. Among the discoveries were sixty golden mummies featuring stunning gilded masks and gilded waistcoats depicting various gods and goddesses.

Their faces glowed in the torchlight as if they were still watching the living. During the Roman period, thirty thousand people lived here, gaining the wealth to afford these elaborate burials from date and grape wine production.

What archaeologists found at this site changed our understanding of the Greco-Roman period forever. It makes you wonder how many thousands more hidden vaults are still resting quietly beneath the shifting sands today.
engage: How would you feel if your torchlight suddenly illuminated sixty golden faces watching you in an ancient tomb?
author: Unknown

hook: Did you know King Tutankhamun was buried with a dagger made from outer space?
article: When excavators unwrapped King Tutankhamun's mummy, they found two daggers inside the wrappings, one made of gold and one of iron. In June 2016, a study using x-ray fluorescence spectrometer analysis confirmed the iron blade contained eleven percent nickel and point six percent cobalt, proving its meteoritic origin.

Iron production did not begin in Egypt until 1200 BC, meaning iron was rarer than gold around 1323 BC. Because of its extreme rarity, the iron dagger was valued on a level equal to that of its ceremonial gold counterpart.
Today, this ancient weapon is displayed at the Grand Egyptian Museum in Cairo. It stands as an astonishing bridge between our world and the cosmos.
engage: What detail about this space-metal dagger surprises you the most?
author: Gary Todd

hook: Did you know ancient Egyptians baked hedgehogs inside clay to remove their sharp spikes?
article: The ancient Egyptian diet was remarkably diverse and included some truly unexpected meals. They even cooked hedgehogs by encasing them in clay and baking them until the spikes fell off.
Ancient Egyptians also regularly ate the tubers, stems, and seeds of papyrus, lotus, and chufa. For dessert, they created sweet treats by mixing honey with ground tiger nuts from the chufa plant.

Chefs prepared these varied ingredients by stewing, baking, boiling, grilling, frying, or roasting. Imagine watching an ancient cook peel away hot baked clay to reveal a dinner completely freed of its prickly outer layer.
engage: How would you feel if you were served a meal baked inside clay like this ancient hedgehog dish?
author: Photo: Andreas Praefcke

hook: Would you stage a massive strike if your boss withheld your beer and bread?
article: About 3,000 years ago during the reign of Ramesses III, royal tomb artisans in the Valley of the Kings completely stopped working. Their sudden walkout happened because their pay of grain rations and barley beer was severely delayed by officials.
Unwilling to starve, the hungry workers marched straight to the funerary temples and staged a massive sit-in. They boldly shouted that hunger and thirst had driven them to protest.
It is incredible to imagine what it felt like to see these artisans stand up to authority in person. Faced with this bold revolt, officials quickly handed over sacks of grain to restore peace.
engage: Would you have walked off the job if your pay of beer and bread was delayed?
author: Egyptian

hook: How did ancient Egyptian artists make a statue's eyes look so terrifyingly realistic?
article: The famous Old Kingdom sculpture known as the Seated Scribe features remarkably lifelike eyes. These eyes were constructed from red-veined white magnesite, polished rock crystal, and secure copper clips.
French archaeologist Auguste Mariette uncovered this stone sculpture at Saqqara on 19 November 1850. Dating to between 2620 and 2325 BC, the statue is held in the Louvre Museum.

Statues of scribes sitting cross-legged with papyrus rolls still look out at us today across millennia with bright crystal eyes. These detailed craftsmanship features offer us an intimate view into three thousand years of continuous daily life.
engage: How would you feel locking eyes with a 4,500-year-old statue made of polished rock crystal?
author: Maler der Grabkammer des Panehsi

hook: Did you know ancient Egyptian priestesses wore sacred religious tattoos over their stomachs?
article: Mummies of the priestesses of Hathor testify that they were decorated with a religious tattoo covering the stomach around the area of the uterus. Sacred tattoos adorned the bodies of these priestesses, connecting their physical form directly to divine fertility and protection.

Priestess of Hathor was the title of the priestess of the goddess Hathor in the Temple of Dendera in Ancient Egypt. After the Middle Kingdom of Egypt, the title of priestess of Hathor was often irregularly awarded to women of the royal family, typically princesses.

Archaeological excavations and preserved papyri collections provide extensive insights into these ancient gender roles. These preserved physical markings show how deeply Egyptian society was rooted in religion and sacred bodily traditions.
engage: What detail about these ancient sacred body tattoos surprised you the most?
author: Egyptian; probably from Hawara, Egypt

hook: Could Queen Nefertiti be resting inches behind King Tut's burial wall?
article: Radar scans inside King Tut's tomb suggest hidden chambers might exist right behind the painted walls of the burial room. The lost resting place of the great queen could be waiting to rewrite history just inches away.

Howard Carter discovered King Tut's tomb in the Valley of the Kings in 1922, sparking a massive global media frenzy. Before young King Tut took the throne, some scholars believe Nefertiti briefly ruled Egypt as a female pharaoh after her husband died.

She had previously ruled as a powerful queen alongside Pharaoh Akhenaten during the wealthiest period of ancient Egyptian history. Decades after Carter's discovery, the possibility remains that her lost mummy is hidden behind a secret wall.
engage: Do you think archaeologists will ever find hidden chambers behind those painted walls?
author: Unknown

hook: Deep under the desert, massive stone coffins were hidden—not for pharaohs, but for bulls.
article: Deep under the desert in pitch-black tunnels, giant stone sarcophagi weighing up to sixty-two tons were hidden away. They were actually constructed to entomb sacred Apis bulls, which were believed to be living gods.

Priests spent sixty-eight days embalming each holy bull before moving the massive stone coffins into underground vaults. Ancient workers lowered these forty-ton boxes into place using levers, winches, and by slowly draining sand beneath them.

Over fourteen hundred years, at least sixty divine bulls received these magnificent royal burials. Walking through those pitch-black underground vaults today brings you face-to-face with the astonishing scale of these sixty-two-ton stone monuments.
engage: Which detail surprises you more: lowering forty-ton stone boxes by draining sand, or spending sixty-eight days embalming a sacred bull?
author: Unknown

hook: Did thousands of sacred ancient Egyptian mummies really get crushed into fertilizer?
article: In 1890, a massive shipment carrying thousands of ancient animal mummies sailed from Egypt to Liverpool, England. Tragically, a large portion of this ancient sacred treasure was sold off to be crushed into agricultural fertilizer.

These bundles were uncovered after an Egyptian farmer digging near Istabl Antar in 1888 stumbled upon hundreds of thousands of cat mummies buried deep in the sand. Ancient worshippers had purchased these embalmed creatures believing they harbored divine souls and secured eternal blessings.

Today, modern CT scans allow scientists to peer inside sealed mummies without unwrapping fragile linen bands. Seeing these delicate, sacred offerings preserved in museums makes the reality of thousands being ground down for farm soil feel completely staggering.
engage: How would you react if you discovered that thousands of ancient sacred treasures were once ground up for farm soil?
